course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Networks of Exchange
unit.description: Study how trade networks connected Afro-Eurasia through goods, technology, states, culture, and environmental change.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Why is “the Silk Road” an incomplete description of exchange after 1200?
choices: It refers to many linked routes and intermediaries rather than one uninterrupted road
It describes only maritime routes between India and East Africa
It means all merchants traveled from China to Europe personally
It refers to a single imperial highway built by the Yuan dynasty
questions.explanation: The network included multiple routes, relay exchange, and regional specialists. It was not one road or a journey completed by every merchant.

questions.prompt: Which development most directly encouraged the growth of Silk Roads exchange?
choices: The disappearance of cities along desert routes
Rising demand for luxury goods combined with safer travel and commercial innovations
A universal ban on merchants using credit
The replacement of all local production with subsistence farming
questions.explanation: Demand created incentives, while security, transport, and commercial practices made more exchange practical.

questions.prompt: What problem did caravanserai primarily help solve?
choices: They replaced all state taxation with private banking
They allowed ships to follow monsoon winds through the desert
They provided organized stopping places for travelers, animals, goods, and information
They guaranteed that every merchant would make a profit
questions.explanation: Caravanserai supported travel and exchange by supplying rest, water, storage, and contact. They did not guarantee profit.

They controlled every Silk Roads route through direct imperial rule
They produced all of the luxury goods traded across Eurasia
Their locations and resources made them useful nodes for trade, services, and cultural exchange
questions.explanation: Both were strategically placed and offered water, food, crafts, markets, and information. Neither controlled every route or produced everything.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best explains how demand could expand long-distance trade?
choices: Demand for luxury goods → fewer artisans → less urban exchange → smaller markets
Demand for luxury goods → increased production → more merchants and transport → larger markets
Increased production → immediate end of farming → total dependence on imports
More markets → elimination of political borders → identical societies
questions.explanation: Demand can encourage production and movement, but it does not eliminate farming, borders, or regional difference.

questions.prompt: How did credit differ from currency?
choices: Credit is always a physical coin; currency is always a written promise
Credit only applied to farmers; currency only applied to rulers
Credit ended the need for trust; currency made trust impossible
Credit is a promise or arrangement for later payment; currency is a medium used to pay
questions.explanation: Credit shifts payment through time or space, while currency is used directly in transactions. Both depend on institutions and trust.

questions.prompt: Which factor would most likely help a trading city grow?
choices: Reliable water, market services, security, and a location where routes intersect
Isolation from routes and refusal to host foreign merchants
A ban on crafts so all residents could farm
A rule that only one product could be sold
questions.explanation: Nodes grow when they can support travelers, goods, information, and production. Isolation and rigid bans work against that role.

They replaced the need for written records with oral promises only

questions.explanation: A bill of exchange could reduce the physical and security costs of moving payment, although trust and institutions remained necessary.

questions.prompt: Which is a historically reasonable limitation of exchange networks?
choices: Trade always produced equal wealth for every region
Trade eliminated local traditions wherever merchants arrived
Trade made political authority irrelevant
Trade could spread ideas and goods while remaining vulnerable to war, disease, weather, and unequal power
questions.explanation: Networks create opportunities and risks. They do not guarantee equality, cultural uniformity, or political decline.

All merchants were soldiers in disguise

Trade had no cultural or economic benefits
questions.explanation: Connectivity has multiple consequences. A balanced claim includes both exchange and its risks.
